taxonomy.subtopic: Michaelis-Menten saturation near the therapeutic range

questions.stem_html: A 34-year-old man with focal epilepsy has taken phenytoin 300 mg daily for 2 years. His serum concentration is 11 mg/L. Because of recurrent seizures, the daily dose is increased modestly. Two weeks later, he has horizontal nystagmus and gait instability, and the serum concentration is 28 mg/L. Adherence and liver function are unchanged. Which pharmacokinetic change most directly explains the disproportionate rise in concentration?

options.text_html: Conversion from capacity-limited elimination to concentration-proportional elimination
Expansion of the apparent volume of distribution due to tissue sequestration
Saturation of hepatic metabolism with a fall in apparent clearance as concentration increases
Increased renal filtration of unbound drug after displacement from albumin
Induction of hepatic enzymes with shortening of the elimination half-life

questions.explanation_html: Phenytoin metabolism follows Michaelis-Menten behavior and can approach saturation within or near the therapeutic range. Once hepatic enzyme capacity is nearly reached, a small increase in daily dose can cause a disproportionately large rise in steady-state concentration. The fraction eliminated per unit time falls, apparent clearance decreases, and neurologic toxicity may develop.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Enzyme induction would increase metabolism and lower, rather than sharply raise, the steady-state concentration.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: An increased volume of distribution would generally lower the measured plasma concentration after a dose and does not explain saturable accumulation.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: The direction is reversed: phenytoin moves from approximately first-order behavior at low concentrations toward capacity-limited, near-zero-order behavior at higher concentrations.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Greater renal filtration would enhance elimination; only a small fraction of phenytoin is excreted unchanged.

questions.educational_objective: Because phenytoin metabolism saturates near therapeutic concentrations, small dose increases can reduce apparent clearance and produce disproportionately large increases in serum concentration.
